e: The size of tomb plots

Tombstones often give the size of the plot: “in fronte pedes XII, in agro pedes XX”, that is, 12 feet along the road and 20 feet back from it. Among the inscriptions from Rome in EDR, 1,345 give both measurements with an intact numeral. One Roman foot is 29.6 cm.

The most common size is 12 × 12 feet (3.55 × 3.55 m): 181 plots, 13% of all. The frontage along the road is exactly 12 feet in 28% of the plots. The median area is 168 square feet (14.7 m²), and the middle half falls between 90 and 256 square feet (7.9–22.4 m²). 605 plots are deeper than they are wide, 427 are square, and 313 are wider than deep.

For age and years of service the median is given, with the middle half and the number of inscriptions in brackets; for the findspot, in brackets: how many inscriptions were found along that road out of those that can be assigned to a road. A dash stands where there are fewer than ten data points.

The epitaphs of the Praetorians cluster near the Castra Praetoria, along the Via Salaria and the Via Nomentana (162 of the 232 that can be assigned to a road). Almost all those of the horse guard come from their cemetery on the Via Labicana (225 of 239). Where both age and length of service are given, the difference is the age at enlistment: from 441 inscriptions the median is 20 years, and the middle half falls between 18 and 21 years.

The curve shows the number of epitaphs in 25-year bands, counted in the same way as on the “Inscriptions” card. The horse guard was organised at the end of the 1st century AD or under Trajan and disbanded, together with the Praetorian Guard, by Constantine in AD 312; accordingly its curve falls in the 2nd–3rd centuries.

The 11th and 12th Praetorian cohorts existed only in the 1st century AD, hence their rarity. Of the urban cohorts, the 10th, 11th, 12th and 14th were stationed in Rome. Of the seven cohorts of the watch, the posts of three are on the map (click the number to jump there); few epitaphs survive for them, and most of what is known about them comes from rosters.

The horse guard was picked from the cavalry units of the Danube and Rhine frontiers (Pannonians, Noricans, Raetians, Batavians); the German bodyguard of the early emperors were Batavians and Ubians; among the fleet soldiers there are Egyptians, Sardinians and Thracian Bessi. Praetorians rarely give an ethnic name; they mostly name their home town.

Limits: only epitaphs are counted, not votive inscriptions or rosters. The unit named in an inscription may be that of the dedicator (the heir or a comrade). Other legions are not included, because in Rome their names mostly occur in lists of officers’ careers.

• The size of tomb plots. Data: EDR (see “Inscriptions”). The summary is our own: the Roman numerals in the phrases “in fronte pedes … in agro pedes …” and “quoquoversus pedes …”, without fragmentary numerals; 1 Roman foot = 29.6 cm (plot/calc.py).

• Soldiers in the epitaphs of Rome. Data: EDR (see “Inscriptions”), the inscriptions from Rome classified as epitaphs. The summary is our own: a search for unit names in the text; age from the numeral after “vixit annis”, length of service from that after “militavit annis” and “stipendiorum”; origin from the ethnic name after “natione” (mil/calc.py).
